extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners who represent clients before the USPTO (practitioners facing or advising on OED disciplinary matters)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and factors used by the USPTO/OED and the USPTO disciplinary court to evaluate practitioner conduct (supervision, diligence, candor, client communication) and to determine sanctions in disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners having direct supervisory authority over a non-practitioner assistant shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that the person’s conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the practitioner. A practitioner shall also be responsible for the misconduct of a non-practitioner assistant if the practitioner has direct supervisory authority over the non-practitioner assistant and fails to take reasonable remedial action. These provisions apply in instances where the non-practitioner assistant is employed or retained by or associated with a practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key elements: (1) direct supervisory authority is a necessary element; (2) practitioner must make reasonable efforts to ensure assistant conduct is compatible with professional obligations; (3) practitioner may be responsible for assistant misconduct if they fail to take reasonable remedial action. Example/authority cited: In re Myers (direct supervisory authority necessary). Anti-pattern: delegating tasks without supervisory authority or remedial follow-up. The Court examined whether respondent had hiring/training authority, whether she dictated how/when work was done, and whether she had meaningful contact with assistants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct requires practitioners to 'act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.' 'Reasonable . . . when used in relation to conduct by a practitioner means the conduct of a reasonably prudent and competent practitioner.' Whether a practitioner fails to act reasonably must be examined in the context of the surrounding circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by examining the specific facts (e.g., whether practitioner knew how filing process was handled, whether she followed up after approval, caseload considerations). Delegation is permitted but only if the attorney maintains direct client relationships, supervises the delegate’s work, and remains responsible for work product (see In re Op. No. 24 of Comm. on Unauthorized Practice of Law). Heavy caseload is not an excuse for failing to use reasonable diligence (e.g., In re Henry Zhang, In re Kroll). Anti-patterns: handing off filing/signature tasks to unsupervised non-practitioner assistants and assuming they performed duties correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions cited: deceit is behavior meant to fool or trick (In re Fred Lane); misrepresentation includes false or misleading assertions and can be conduct, not just words (Black’s Law Dictionary). Evaluation requires evidence of intentional or knowing misconduct. Anti-pattern: knowingly causing filings with false signatures or intentionally misleading the USPTO or clients. Absent actual knowledge, negligent failures typically are not treated as intentional deceit under this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep clients reasonably informed and to explain matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) & (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner is required to 'keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter.' In addition, a practitioner must also explain the matter 'to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by assessing whether, once on notice of a problem, the practitioner investigated and communicated with clients (e.g., after receiving an RFI). Examples of failures: not notifying clients that their signatures may have been impermissibly entered, or sending communications that omit the true purpose of inquiries. Good practice: timely, clear disclosure of potential harm so clients can make informed decisions and mitigate damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes 'conduct which impedes or subverts the process of resolving disputes' or 'frustrates the fair balance of interests or 'justice' essential to litigation or other proceedings.' Also includes behavior that negatively impacts public perception of the courts or legal profession or undermines public confidence in the legal system (cases: In re Friedman; Att’y Grievance Comm’n v. Rand). In application, negligent failures that affect only the practitioner’s clients—but not the system or public confidence—may not rise to this violation (see In re Kroll).

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the USPTO; duty to correct and disclose (37 C.F.R. § 11.303)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not knowingly fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the USPTO (§11.303(a)(1)). If a practitioner knows evidence they offered is false, they must take reasonable remedial measures, which may include disclosure to the USPTO (§11.303(a)(3)). If a practitioner knows a person intends to engage in fraudulent conduct, the practitioner shall take remedial measures such as notifying the USPTO (§11.303(b)). In ex parte proceedings, the practitioner must inform the USPTO of all material facts known that will enable an informed decision (§11.303(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An essential element is actual knowledge (definition in §11.1). Knowledge may be inferred from circumstances, but findings require clear and convincing evidence. Practical implication: nondisclosure or failure to correct requires proof that the practitioner knew the statement was false or had actual knowledge of the fraud; mere negligence or lack of diligence does not automatically establish this violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/threshold of 'knowledge' (37 C.F.R. § 11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Know' is defined as having 'actual knowledge of the fact in question.' The definition further explains that 'a person’s knowledge may be inferred from the circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to determine duties that hinge on the practitioner's knowledge (e.g., duty to disclose, duty to correct). The Office requires actual knowledge for certain remedial duties; circumstantial evidence can support inference of knowledge but must meet evidentiary standards applied by the tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for disciplinary proceedings (35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.34(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 32 establishes a two-stage limitations period: a proceeding shall be commenced not later than the earlier of (1) 10 years after the misconduct occurred, or (2) 1 year after the date on which the misconduct is made known to an office or employee of the Office. The USPTO regulation requires a complaint be filed within one year after the OED Director receives a 'grievance' forming the basis of the complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.34(d)). A 'grievance' is 'a written submission from any source received by the OED Director that presents possible grounds for discipline of a specified practitioner' (37 C.F.R. § 11.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination focuses on when the misconduct was 'made known' to OED (i.e., the date a grievance was received). Burden of proving statute-of-limitations defense rests on respondent. Application requires specific evidence identifying a grievance tied to the practitioner; speculative or indirect evidence is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard: clear and convincing evidence required
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings of misconduct in these disciplinary proceedings are required to be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing evidence means evidence 'of such weight that it produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy, as to the truth of the allegations' (citation: Jimenez v. DaimlerChrysler). The Court applied this standard when weighing testimony, documentary evidence (e.g., XML signature methods, IP address data), and declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider: (1) Whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) The existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary purpose of discipline is protection of the public and the bar, not punishment. The Court considers aggravating/mitigating facts and often looks to the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions. Examples of aggravating factors noted: pattern of misconduct (multiple instances over time), multiple offenses. Mitigating factors include following employer procedures or absence of intent. The Court balanced these factors in determining appropriate sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiduciary duty to clients (general duty/ethical baseline)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner-client relationship is a fiduciary relationship in which the practitioner owes the client a duty to represent his or her interests diligently and in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breach of fiduciary duty (e.g., failing to ensure clients' matters are handled with reasonable diligence, failing to inform clients of problems) weighs heavily in sanction analysis. Authorities cited describe the special confidence and trust inherent in the relationship. Assessment considers whether conduct harmed clients or exposed them to potential injury (e.g., risk of trademark cancellation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negligence as a ground for discipline and its definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Negligence is defined as 'the failure to take reasonable care.' Practitioner conduct may be characterized as negligent (as opposed to intentional) where the practitioner fails to exercise reasonable care in supervision, filing, or client communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tribunal examines whether the practitioner exercised reasonable care (e.g., made inquiries, supervised delegates, followed up after approval). Examples: allowing assistants over whom the attorney had no supervisory authority to collect signatures and file documents without follow-up. Negligent conduct may lead to discipline but is assessed differently than intentional misconduct when considering sanctions and violations requiring scienter (e.g., candor rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors in sanction analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court evaluates aggravating and mitigating factors when deciding sanctions; aggravating factors include patterns of misconduct and multiple offenses, while mitigating factors may include lack of intent, following employer procedures, or other circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative aggravating factors from the record: pattern of misconduct (sixteen impermissibly signed documents over five months) and multiple rule violations (failure to act with diligence and failure to inform clients). Mitigating facts may reduce culpability (e.g., following firm procedures, lack of managerial authority, absence of actual knowledge). The ABA Standards are consulted for structuring this analysis.
